lessons.title: Plato & Aristotle
lessons.summary: The theory of Forms, the allegory of the cave, and Aristotle's critique and empiricism.
lessons.script:
Plato held that the changing physical world is a shadow of a higher realm of unchanging Forms (Ideas). True knowledge is recollection of these Forms. The Allegory of the Cave dramatises the philosopher's ascent from illusion to the Form of the Good.

Aristotle, Plato's pupil, rejected a separate realm of Forms. For him, form and matter are united in things (hylomorphism). He grounded knowledge in observation and built systematic logic (the syllogism), ethics (the doctrine of the mean), and metaphysics (the four causes). This Plato-Aristotle contrast — rationalist idealism vs empirical realism — is a recurring theme in the whole subject.
keyPoints: Plato: world of Forms; knowledge as recollection.
Allegory of the Cave depicts ascent to the Form of the Good.
Core contrast: rationalist idealism vs empirical realism.

questions.stem: The Allegory of the Cave is associated with:
questions.explanation: The Allegory of the Cave appears in Plato's Republic and illustrates the ascent from illusion to knowledge of the Forms.

questions.stem: Aristotle's view that form and matter are united in a substance is called:

lessons.title: Pressure Belts & Global Winds
lessons.summary: Seven pressure belts, the Coriolis effect, and the planetary wind system.
lessons.script:
Differential heating of the Earth creates seven alternating pressure belts: the Equatorial Low, two Subtropical Highs, two Subpolar Lows, and two Polar Highs. Air moves from high to low pressure, but the Coriolis effect (due to the Earth's rotation) deflects it — to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern.

This produces the three planetary wind systems: the Trade Winds (subtropical high to equatorial low), the Westerlies (subtropical high to subpolar low), and the Polar Easterlies. Seasonal shifts of these belts with the apparent movement of the Sun help drive monsoons.
keyPoints: Seven pressure belts, alternating high and low.
Coriolis effect deflects winds right (N) / left (S).
Three wind systems: Trades, Westerlies, Polar Easterlies.
Belt shifts with the Sun drive seasonal monsoons.

questions.stem: In the Northern Hemisphere, the Coriolis effect deflects moving air to the:
questions.explanation: Due to the Earth's rotation, the Coriolis effect deflects winds to the right in the Northern Hemisphere.

modules.title: Module 1 — Speaking with Structure

lessons.title: The PREP Framework
lessons.summary: Point, Reason, Example, Point — a simple structure for clear spoken answers.
lessons.script:
Under pressure, most people ramble. The PREP framework keeps you organised: state your POINT first, give a REASON, support it with an EXAMPLE, then restate the POINT. In an interview, this turns a vague answer into a tight 30-45 second response.

Practise by taking any opinion question ('Should cities ban private cars in the centre?') and answering in PREP order out loud. The discipline of leading with your point — rather than thinking aloud — is what makes you sound confident and decisive.
keyPoints: Lead with the point; don't think aloud.
Practise on opinion questions out loud.

questions.stem: In the PREP framework, what comes immediately after stating your Point?
questions.explanation: PREP stands for Point, Reason, Example, Point — the Reason directly supports your opening point.
